fixes.explanation: Right. Asaph says, “…then I would have betrayed Your children.” He's got all these thoughts in his head, but he knows what talking that way would do. Some words are better kept in the oven until they're done, friend.
Friends don't come up here, friend. Asaph says, “…then I would have betrayed Your children.” The text names God's children, not a friend list. That's the cost he names.
No king in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “…then I would have betrayed Your children.” The weight here is on God's children. A king never enters the picture.

That's it: “They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men.” You know that coworker who never gets handed the hard assignments while everybody else's desk is buried? That's how Asaph sees them. Life's weight just seems to skip them.
Right, friend. Asaph says, “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.” Mocking, malice and threats are what he names. I think that's the part that stings.

Not here, friend. Asaph says, “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.” Mocking, malice and threats are what he names, not whispering and hiding. The next verse says, “They set their mouths against the heavens…”

I get why it sounds possible, friend, but it's the other way around. Asaph says, “They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.” Their talk doesn't leave heaven out. Their mouths are set against it, and their tongues strut across the earth.
Right, it's False. The verse says, “They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.” So heaven isn't left out of their big talk, friend. It's right in it.

Repaying doesn't come up in their question, friend. They say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” Their whole question is whether God knows anything at all. Asaph is just repeating what they say, and I'd call that a bold thing to say out loud.
Plans? No blueprints in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “…then I discerned their end.” He didn't get a peek at their calendar. He saw where they end up.
True. Asaph says, “Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin.” I think it looked like solid ground from the outside. Now he sees it differently.
Yes, “…but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” Asaph's own heart may give out, but he says God is its strength. A portion is what is his, and he says it's God Himself.

Prosper isn't in this verse, friend. Earlier Asaph talks about the prosperity of the wicked, but here he says, “My flesh and my heart may fail…” He's admitting he can give out. The next part names God as his strength.
Wealth is what Asaph saw in the wicked at the start, friend. By the end he says, “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God.” His eyes have landed on God.
A great name doesn't show up in this psalm, friend. Asaph says, “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God.” That's the good thing he lands on. The search ends with God, not with a name.
